# A Supply-Chain Resilience Strategy for Critical Semiconductor Materials

## Executive Recommendation

The semiconductor materials supply chain in 2026 is the most consequential single point of failure in the global technology stack that is not yet under systematic enterprise risk management. While fabs, lithography systems, and design IP receive the lion's share of strategic attention, the underlying layer of specialty gases and photoresists — often sourced from three or four producers in three or four countries — has structural concentration that would survive any one disruption but is now being tested by correlated disruptions: simultaneous export controls from competing geopolitical blocs, capacity consolidation among specialist chemical suppliers, and qualification timelines that are longer than the news cycle of any one trade dispute. The financial cost of a six-month disruption to advanced-node wafer output vastly exceeds the cost of a five-year optionality-rich supply agreement, but the trade-off is not framed in those terms in most finance committees, which is the first problem to solve.

The strategic call is to move from a single-toolkit mindset ("dual-source everything that matters") to a portfolio approach that matches the depth of resilience investment to the criticality and risk profile of each material, and to restructure the supplier-commitment economics so that suppliers can make capacity decisions with confidence while the buyer's finance function retains demand flexibility.

Five operating principles should govern the program:

1. **Tier every critical material by existential risk, not by spend.** Some materials account for a small fraction of cost-of-goods but are irreplaceable in the process recipe; others are large-spend but well-supplied. Resilience investment should be driven by a Criticality × Concentration × Geopolitical-Exposure score, not by spend.

2. **Use a portfolio of dual-sourcing approaches, not a single template.** Full dual-sourcing (two actively used suppliers), qualified dual-sourcing (primary-secondary split), capacity-qualified backup (qualified at lower fidelity, lower cost), and formulation-qualified backup (different chemistry or process route) each carry different cost-risk profiles. The right choice depends on material tier and supplier economics.

3. **Restructure supplier commitments around optionality-rich contracts that both sides can live with.** Capacity reservation agreements, volume commitments with make-up rights, joint capacity investments with shared risk, government-backed offtake facilities, and pre-purchase storage contracts can shift risk allocation in ways that suppliers accept and finance tolerates. The conventional take-or-pay model is neither the only nor the best instrument.

4. **Build a permanent pre-qualification pipeline that runs ahead of geopolitical risk.** The 12-24 month qualification timeline is the binding constraint on responsiveness. A standing qualification program for backup suppliers — funded as a recurring opex line, not a crisis-driven capex spike — converts the binding constraint into an ongoing capability.

5. **Hold strategic inventory and design process flexibility for Tier 0 and Tier 1 materials.** Just-in-time inventory discipline has produced enormous working-capital efficiency, but for the materials where a six-week supply gap would halt production, six to twelve months of strategic inventory is an insurance premium worth paying. Process flexibility — the ability to run on a backup material specification without re-qualifying the entire process — multiplies the value of every other resilience investment.

The remainder of this strategy works through the material-risk tiering, the dual-sourcing portfolio, the qualification acceleration, the commitment-economics restructuring, the inventory and demand-flex levers, the operational governance, and the implementation roadmap required to make this real.

---

## 1. The 2026 Semiconductor Materials Risk Landscape

Four structural shifts define the present risk environment and shape the strategy.

**Export-control regimes have become correlated, not independent.** The post-2018 trajectory of US export controls on advanced semiconductor manufacturing to China, China's retaliatory controls on critical materials (gallium, germanium, antimony, graphite, and various rare-earth compounds), Japan's 2019 export-controls precedent with South Korea, and the broader Wassenaar Arrangement controls have created a regime in which a single bilateral incident can produce simultaneous restrictions across multiple jurisdictions. For semiconductor materials, this means that supplier concentration in any one country is a more acute risk than it would have been five years earlier, because the probability of any one country imposing controls has risen.

**Supplier consolidation has reduced redundancy in critical chemistries.** Specialty gas production and photoresist synthesis are increasingly concentrated. The advanced photoresist market is dominated by four Japanese firms (JSR, Tokyo Ohka Kogyo, Shin-Etsu Chemical, Sumitomo Chemical) with limited non-Japanese competition for EUV and advanced ArF immersion grades. The noble-gas supply chain, which was significantly Ukrainian and Russian until 2022, has been re-architected by the major gas companies — Air Liquide, Linde, Air Products — with new capacity in the United States, Qatar, and elsewhere, but the recovery took 24-36 months and the lessons are still fresh. Materials like tungsten hexafluoride, certain dopant gases, and high-purity hydrogen fluoride have similarly concentrated supply.

**The fab-capacity build-out is running ahead of materials-supply redundancy.** The CHIPS Act in the United States, the European Chips Act, Korean K-CHIPS, Japanese semiconductor stimulus, and various other national programs have driven a fab construction wave through 2024-2026. New fabs in Arizona, Ohio, Germany, Japan, and Korea will come online with substantial new demand for advanced materials, competing with existing fabs for the same supplier capacity. Suppliers will, in many cases, be in a position to demand stricter offtake commitments to finance expansion — which is the exact negotiating environment the original prompt describes.

**Qualification timelines have not compressed materially in a decade, while disruption cycles have compressed dramatically.** A typical photoresist qualification at an advanced node still takes 12-24 months including initial screening, sample evaluation, recipe-matching tests, wafer-level reliability testing, statistical process control validation, and customer-end product qualification. Specialty gas qualification is somewhat faster but still measured in quarters. Meanwhile, the cycle from a trade dispute flaring to an export-control announcement has been measured in weeks; from an announcement to enforcement, in days. The mismatch is structural and cannot be solved by emergency procurement; it requires a standing capability.

These shifts together mean that resilience investment must be designed against a worst-case scenario in which two of the supplier's host countries impose export controls in the same quarter, while a third supplier is undergoing post-acquisition capacity reallocation, while the buyer is qualifying a fourth supplier that has been waiting for an offtake commitment for eighteen months. The strategy below is designed to function in that scenario.

---

## 2. Risk-Tiered Material Framework

### 2.1 The Three-Dimensional Tiering

Every critical material should be scored on three axes:

| Axis | Question | Score Range |
|---|---|---|
| **Criticality** | What happens to production if this material is unavailable for 90 days? | 1 (manageable yield loss) to 5 (production halt) |
| **Concentration** | How many qualified suppliers exist, and in how many distinct geopolitical blocs? | 1 (5+ suppliers, 3+ blocs) to 5 (single supplier, single bloc) |
| **Geopolitical Exposure** | How likely is each supplier's host country to impose export controls in the next 36 months? | 1 (stable, friendly) to 5 (active dispute, controls in force) |

Composite Risk Score = weighted sum, with Criticality and Concentration weighted higher than Geopolitical Exposure (since the latter changes faster than the former). Tier the materials as:

- **Tier 0 (Existential):** Composite score 13-15. No substitution, no real alternative supplier. Example: certain EUV photoresists for sub-3nm production, certain advanced-node dopant gases.
- **Tier 1 (Critical):** Composite score 10-12. Limited alternatives, substitution possible but costly and time-consuming. Example: most advanced ArF immersion photoresists, noble gases for excimer lasers, certain high-purity etchant gases.
- **Tier 2 (Important):** Composite score 7-9. Multiple qualified suppliers, but concentration is high. Example: standard ArF photoresists, common specialty gases, certain CMP slurries.
- **Tier 3 (Manageable):** Composite score 4-6. Adequate competitive supply. Example: commodity gases, bulk chemicals, mature-node photoresists.

The tier drives the resilience investment intensity, not the spend level. A Tier 0 material with a small annual spend should receive more resilience investment than a Tier 3 material with ten times the spend.

### 2.2 Tier-Specific Resilience Posture

| Tier | Dual-Sourcing Posture | Qualification Status | Inventory Posture | Commitment Posture |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tier 0 (Existential) | Full dual-source with formulation backup where possible | Two suppliers fully qualified, third at capacity-qualified status | 6-12 months strategic stockpile | Long-term offtake with capacity reservation and government co-financing where available |
| Tier 1 (Critical) | Full or qualified dual-source | Two suppliers qualified | 3-6 months inventory | Volume commitments with make-up rights |
| Tier 2 (Important) | Qualified dual-source or capacity backup | Primary + one backup qualified | 1-3 months inventory | Standard contracts with optional extension |
| Tier 3 (Manageable) | Single-source acceptable for non-critical applications | Standard qualification | Just-in-time | Spot contracts with relationship continuity |

The rest of this strategy works primarily against Tier 0 and Tier 1 materials, where the cost of disruption is highest and where the supplier-commitment economics are most acute.

---

## 3. The Dual-Sourcing Decision Matrix

### 3.1 The Portfolio of Approaches

Dual-sourcing in semiconductors is commonly understood as qualifying two suppliers and splitting volume roughly 50/50. In practice, this is one of five approaches, and the others often deliver better cost-risk profiles for specific material tiers:

**Approach A — Active Dual-Sourcing (50/50):** Two qualified suppliers, volume split to keep both engaged and qualified. Highest resilience but highest cost (each supplier carries fixed-cost burden at lower volume, qualification is fully duplicated, and process control becomes more complex). Justified for Tier 0 materials where the cost of a single-supplier failure is catastrophic and where both suppliers have the capacity to support full demand.

**Approach B — Primary/Backup Split (80/20 or 90/10):** Primary supplier carries most volume; backup supplier is fully qualified but operates at low utilization to maintain readiness. Backup supplier typically charges a readiness premium. Lower cost than full dual-sourcing but requires the backup to genuinely maintain capability (which is itself a contract negotiation problem).

**Approach C — Capacity-Qualified Backup:** Backup supplier is qualified at lower fidelity — capable of producing material that meets specifications but not fully integrated into the production process control system. Faster to ramp in a disruption, lower ongoing qualification cost. Appropriate for Tier 1 materials where the cost of a slower-than-usual qualification during a disruption is acceptable.

**Approach D — Formulation-Qualified Backup:** Backup is a different chemistry, different process route, or different impurity profile that meets the same functional requirement but with a distinct supply chain. This is the highest-cost, lowest-utilization backup but the most resilient to geopolitical shocks because it does not share any input supply chain with the primary. Appropriate for Tier 0 materials where the risk is correlated across the primary supply base.

**Approach E — Capacity Reservation without Active Qualification:** Buyer pays a reservation fee to a potential supplier for guaranteed capacity access in a disruption, without going through full qualification. Activation requires emergency qualification. Used as a third tier of insurance below Approaches B/C/D.

### 3.2 The Selection Matrix

| Material Tier | Recommended Approach | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Tier 0 (Existential) | A + D (Active dual-source + formulation backup) | Maximum resilience; formulation backup hedges correlated supply risk |
| Tier 1 (Critical) | B or C (Primary/backup split or capacity-qualified backup) | Cost-efficient for high-concentration materials where full dual-sourcing is uneconomic |
| Tier 2 (Important) | C (Capacity-qualified backup) | Single fully qualified primary plus a qualified backup at lower fidelity |
| Tier 3 (Manageable) | Single-source with relationship continuity | Standard procurement discipline |

The decision must also factor supplier-specific dynamics: a supplier who is itself capacity-constrained will resist Approach A; a supplier with idle capacity may welcome it; a supplier in a high-geopolitical-risk jurisdiction may prefer Approach C over A because they understand the buyer's risk. The right configuration is bilateral.

---

## 4. Qualification Acceleration Strategies

The 12-24 month qualification timeline is the binding constraint on responsiveness. Three structural levers can compress it materially.

### 4.1 Parallel Qualification with Stage-Gate Investment

The traditional model is sequential: qualify Supplier A first, then start qualifying Supplier B only after A is fully integrated. This guarantees that any disruption during A's qualification delays B's start by the full timeline. The alternative is parallel qualification of two suppliers from the outset, with a stage gate at month 6-9 that decides which to continue investing in and which to demote to a lower-tier backup.

This requires up-front qualification capex on two suppliers before either is needed for production. The cost is real but bounded — qualification costs are dominated by engineering time, not materials, and the marginal cost of qualifying a second supplier in parallel is significantly less than 2× the cost of qualifying one sequentially. The benefit is that, at any point in the program, two suppliers are partially qualified, and the time to full qualification of the backup is compressed from 18 months to perhaps 4-6 months.

### 4.2 Tiered Qualification Fidelity

Full process-of-record qualification at an advanced node is rigorous precisely because the cost of failure is high. But there are several intermediate qualification states that provide meaningful insurance at much lower cost:

- **Material-specification qualified:** Supplier can produce material meeting the published specification, but has not been integrated into the production process control system. Useful as a Tier C backup.
- **Wafer-level qualified:** Material has been tested at wafer scale with positive results, but not in volume production. Faster to ramp.
- **Reference-customer qualified:** Supplier has been qualified by a peer fab at the same node. Qualification data can sometimes be shared under NDA, compressing the buyer's qualification by 6-12 months.

For Tier 0 and Tier 1 materials, building a portfolio of suppliers at different qualification fidelities is a higher-leverage investment than over-investing in one supplier's full qualification.

### 4.3 Industry-Consortium Qualification Data

Several industry consortia — including SEMI's supplier-evaluation programs, various national materials initiatives, and customer-led consortia — share pre-qualification data among members. The economics work because every fab faces the same qualification cost, and the marginal value of any one fab's qualification data to the others is high.

Where such consortia do not exist for a given material, the buyer should consider founding one — even a small consortium of 3-5 peer fabs can dramatically reduce the qualification cost per member, and it creates a forum for sharing capacity intelligence, demand forecasts, and supplier risk assessments. CHIPS Act and EU Chips Act funding has been allocated to some of these consortia; the buyer should explore them actively.

### 4.4 Pre-Qualification of Strategic Materials

The cleanest answer to the qualification timeline is to start qualifying backup suppliers *before* they are needed for production, on a continuous rolling basis. The platform should fund a standing qualification program — perhaps 5-10% of the materials-procurement budget — that continuously moves potential backup suppliers through partial qualification, even when there is no immediate production need.

This converts the 18-month timeline from a response into a continuous operational capability. When geopolitical conditions change, the buyer has a bench of partially qualified backup suppliers ready to be promoted to full qualification in months rather than a year-plus.

The cost is recurring opex rather than crisis-driven capex. Finance is more comfortable with this because the spending is predictable and the value (option value on supply continuity) is preserved across cycles.

---

## 5. Long-Term Commitment Economics and Contract Structures

This is the section the original prompt identifies as the central problem: alternative suppliers are reluctant to commit capacity without long-term offtake agreements, but finance resists long-term commitments because they lock in costs and reduce flexibility. The resolution is not to choose between these positions but to restructure the commitments so that they share risk appropriately.

### 5.1 The Underlying Economic Problem

Suppliers in specialty gases and photoresists face a specific cost profile: high fixed cost (specialized plant, cleanrooms, analytical equipment), moderate variable cost (raw materials, energy, labor), and steep learning-curve effects at the customer end. Capacity decisions are lumpy — a new gas plant or photoresist synthesis line is a $100M-$1B investment, with lead times of 18-36 months and utilization that depends on committed offtake.

Buyers face a different cost profile: high volume variability (driven by fab utilization, technology node transitions, end-market demand), need for cost reduction over time (the industry price-curve forces it), and limited ability to predict demand 5 years out (the fab itself may not exist 5 years out, or may be running different processes).

The standard take-or-pay contract fails both sides: the supplier gets demand certainty they cannot actually use (because if the buyer's demand drops, the supplier's plant still operates and the supplier can sell elsewhere, often at lower margins), and the buyer pays for capacity they don't need.

### 5.2 A Toolkit of Optionality-Rich Contract Structures

The following structures can be deployed selectively across the material portfolio.

**Capacity Reservation Agreement (CRA).** The buyer pays a recurring reservation fee (typically 5-15% of the committed capacity's price) in exchange for guaranteed access to capacity in a disruption. The reservation fee compensates the supplier for holding capacity idle; the buyer retains the right to purchase or not purchase at the contracted price, with a cap on the upside (often 110-130% of the contract price). This is essentially a put option on capacity access.

Best for: Tier 0 and Tier 1 materials where the supplier has idle or expandable capacity and the buyer values disruption insurance over price certainty.

**Volume Commitment with Make-up Rights.** The buyer commits to a baseline volume (say 70% of expected demand) over a multi-year period, with the right to take additional volume up to a cap at a contracted price, and the right to under-take the baseline in a given year and make up the volume in a subsequent year. The supplier gets revenue visibility on the baseline; the buyer gets demand flexibility on the upside.

Best for: Tier 1 materials where the buyer has reasonable demand visibility but capacity risk is real.

**Joint Capacity Investment.** The buyer and supplier jointly invest in new capacity, with the buyer's contribution (perhaps 30-50%) treated as a prepayment that is recovered through a discounted price schedule over the contract term. This is a true partnership structure that aligns incentives across the entire investment cycle.

Best for: Tier 0 materials where the supplier is willing to expand but cannot finance the expansion alone. Often combined with government loan guarantees or co-financing from CHIPS Act-style programs.

**Pre-Purchase Storage Contract.** The buyer pays now for material that will be delivered and stored over a 12-36 month period. The supplier uses the prepayment to finance capacity expansion; the buyer stores the material at a third-party logistics provider or in their own warehouse.

# A Supply-Chain Resilience Strategy for Critical Semiconductor Materials

## Executive Recommendation

The semiconductor materials supply chain in 2026 is the most consequential single point of failure in the global technology stack that is not yet under systematic enterprise risk management. While fabs, lithography systems, and design IP receive the lion's share of strategic attention, the underlying layer of specialty gases and photoresists — often sourced from three or four producers in three or four countries — has structural concentration that would survive any one disruption but is now being tested by correlated disruptions: simultaneous export controls from competing geopolitical blocs, capacity consolidation among specialist chemical suppliers, and qualification timelines that are longer than the news cycle of any one trade dispute. The financial cost of a six-month disruption to advanced-node wafer output vastly exceeds the cost of a five-year optionality-rich supply agreement, but the trade-off is not framed in those terms in most finance committees, which is the first problem to solve.

The strategic call is to move from a single-toolkit mindset ("dual-source everything that matters") to a portfolio approach that matches the depth of resilience investment to the criticality and risk profile of each material, and to restructure the supplier-commitment economics so that suppliers can make capacity decisions with confidence while the buyer's finance function retains demand flexibility.

Five operating principles should govern the program:

1. **Tier every critical material by existential risk, not by spend.** Some materials account for a small fraction of cost-of-goods but are irreplaceable in the process recipe; others are large-spend but well-supplied. Resilience investment should be driven by a Criticality × Concentration × Geopolitical-Exposure score, not by spend.

2. **Use a portfolio of dual-sourcing approaches, not a single template.** Full dual-sourcing (two actively used suppliers), qualified dual-sourcing (primary-secondary split), capacity-qualified backup (qualified at lower fidelity, lower cost), and formulation-qualified backup (different chemistry or process route) each carry different cost-risk profiles. The right choice depends on material tier and supplier economics.

3. **Restructure supplier commitments around optionality-rich contracts that both sides can live with.** Capacity reservation agreements, volume commitments with make-up rights, joint capacity investments with shared risk, government-backed offtake facilities, and pre-purchase storage contracts can shift risk allocation in ways that suppliers accept and finance tolerates. The conventional take-or-pay model is neither the only nor the best instrument.

4. **Build a permanent pre-qualification pipeline that runs ahead of geopolitical risk.** The 12-24 month qualification timeline is the binding constraint on responsiveness. A standing qualification program for backup suppliers — funded as a recurring opex line, not a crisis-driven capex spike — converts the binding constraint into an ongoing capability.

5. **Hold strategic inventory and design process flexibility for Tier 0 and Tier 1 materials.** Just-in-time inventory discipline has produced enormous working-capital efficiency, but for the materials where a six-week supply gap would halt production, six to twelve months of strategic inventory is an insurance premium worth paying. Process flexibility — the ability to run on a backup material specification without re-qualifying the entire process — multiplies the value of every other resilience investment.

The remainder of this strategy works through the material-risk tiering, the dual-sourcing portfolio, the qualification acceleration, the commitment-economics restructuring, the inventory and demand-flex levers, the operational governance, and the implementation roadmap required to make this real.

---

## 1. The 2026 Semiconductor Materials Risk Landscape

Four structural shifts define the present risk environment and shape the strategy.

**Export-control regimes have become correlated, not independent.** The post-2018 trajectory of US export controls on advanced semiconductor manufacturing to China, China's retaliatory controls on critical materials (gallium, germanium, antimony, graphite, and various rare-earth compounds), Japan's 2019 export-controls precedent with South Korea, and the broader Wassenaar Arrangement controls have created a regime in which a single bilateral incident can produce simultaneous restrictions across multiple jurisdictions. For semiconductor materials, this means that supplier concentration in any one country is a more acute risk than it would have been five years earlier, because the probability of any one country imposing controls has risen.

**Supplier consolidation has reduced redundancy in critical chemistries.** Specialty gas production and photoresist synthesis are increasingly concentrated. The advanced photoresist market is dominated by four Japanese firms (JSR, Tokyo Ohka Kogyo, Shin-Etsu Chemical, Sumitomo Chemical) with limited non-Japanese competition for EUV and advanced ArF immersion grades. The noble-gas supply chain, which was significantly Ukrainian and Russian until 2022, has been re-architected by the major gas companies — Air Liquide, Linde, Air Products — with new capacity in the United States, Qatar, and elsewhere, but the recovery took 24-36 months and the lessons are still fresh. Materials like tungsten hexafluoride, certain dopant gases, and high-purity hydrogen fluoride have similarly concentrated supply.

**The fab-capacity build-out is running ahead of materials-supply redundancy.** The CHIPS Act in the United States, the European Chips Act, Korean K-CHIPS, Japanese semiconductor stimulus, and various other national programs have driven a fab construction wave through 2024-2026. New fabs in Arizona, Ohio, Germany, Japan, and Korea will come online with substantial new demand for advanced materials, competing with existing fabs for the same supplier capacity. Suppliers will, in many cases, be in a position to demand stricter offtake commitments to finance expansion — which is the exact negotiating environment the original prompt describes.

**Qualification timelines have not compressed materially in a decade, while disruption cycles have compressed dramatically.** A typical photoresist qualification at an advanced node still takes 12-24 months including initial screening, sample evaluation, recipe-matching tests, wafer-level reliability testing, statistical process control validation, and customer-end product qualification. Specialty gas qualification is somewhat faster but still measured in quarters. Meanwhile, the cycle from a trade dispute flaring to an export-control announcement has been measured in weeks; from an announcement to enforcement, in days. The mismatch is structural and cannot be solved by emergency procurement; it requires a standing capability.

These shifts together mean that resilience investment must be designed against a worst-case scenario in which two of the supplier's host countries impose export controls in the same quarter, while a third supplier is undergoing post-acquisition capacity reallocation, while the buyer is qualifying a fourth supplier that has been waiting for an offtake commitment for eighteen months. The strategy below is designed to function in that scenario.

---

## 2. Risk-Tiered Material Framework

### 2.1 The Three-Dimensional Tiering

Every critical material should be scored on three axes:

| Axis | Question | Score Range |
|---|---|---|
| **Criticality** | What happens to production if this material is unavailable for 90 days? | 1 (manageable yield loss) to 5 (production halt) |
| **Concentration** | How many qualified suppliers exist, and in how many distinct geopolitical blocs? | 1 (5+ suppliers, 3+ blocs) to 5 (single supplier, single bloc) |
| **Geopolitical Exposure** | How likely is each supplier's host country to impose export controls in the next 36 months? | 1 (stable, friendly) to 5 (active dispute, controls in force) |

Composite Risk Score = weighted sum, with Criticality and Concentration weighted higher than Geopolitical Exposure (since the latter changes faster than the former). Tier the materials as:

- **Tier 0 (Existential):** Composite score 13-15. No substitution, no real alternative supplier. Example: certain EUV photoresists for sub-3nm production, certain advanced-node dopant gases.
- **Tier 1 (Critical):** Composite score 10-12. Limited alternatives, substitution possible but costly and time-consuming. Example: most advanced ArF immersion photoresists, noble gases for excimer lasers, certain high-purity etchant gases.
- **Tier 2 (Important):** Composite score 7-9. Multiple qualified suppliers, but concentration is high. Example: standard ArF photoresists, common specialty gases, certain CMP slurries.
- **Tier 3 (Manageable):** Composite score 4-6. Adequate competitive supply. Example: commodity gases, bulk chemicals, mature-node photoresists.

The tier drives the resilience investment intensity, not the spend level. A Tier 0 material with a small annual spend should receive more resilience investment than a Tier 3 material with ten times the spend.

### 2.2 Tier-Specific Resilience Posture

| Tier | Dual-Sourcing Posture | Qualification Status | Inventory Posture | Commitment Posture |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tier 0 (Existential) | Full dual-source with formulation backup where possible | Two suppliers fully qualified, third at capacity-qualified status | 6-12 months strategic stockpile | Long-term offtake with capacity reservation and government co-financing where available |
| Tier 1 (Critical) | Full or qualified dual-source | Two suppliers qualified | 3-6 months inventory | Volume commitments with make-up rights |
| Tier 2 (Important) | Qualified dual-source or capacity backup | Primary + one backup qualified | 1-3 months inventory | Standard contracts with optional extension |
| Tier 3 (Manageable) | Single-source acceptable for non-critical applications | Standard qualification | Just-in-time | Spot contracts with relationship continuity |

The rest of this strategy works primarily against Tier 0 and Tier 1 materials, where the cost of disruption is highest and where the supplier-commitment economics are most acute.

---

## 3. The Dual-Sourcing Decision Matrix

### 3.1 The Portfolio of Approaches

Dual-sourcing in semiconductors is commonly understood as qualifying two suppliers and splitting volume roughly 50/50. In practice, this is one of five approaches, and the others often deliver better cost-risk profiles for specific material tiers:

**Approach A — Active Dual-Sourcing (50/50):** Two qualified suppliers, volume split to keep both engaged and qualified. Highest resilience but highest cost (each supplier carries fixed-cost burden at lower volume, qualification is fully duplicated, and process control becomes more complex). Justified for Tier 0 materials where the cost of a single-supplier failure is catastrophic and where both suppliers have the capacity to support full demand.

**Approach B — Primary/Backup Split (80/20 or 90/10):** Primary supplier carries most volume; backup supplier is fully qualified but operates at low utilization to maintain readiness. Backup supplier typically charges a readiness premium. Lower cost than full dual-sourcing but requires the backup to genuinely maintain capability (which is itself a contract negotiation problem).

**Approach C — Capacity-Qualified Backup:** Backup supplier is qualified at lower fidelity — capable of producing material that meets specifications but not fully integrated into the production process control system. Faster to ramp in a disruption, lower ongoing qualification cost. Appropriate for Tier 1 materials where the cost of a slower-than-usual qualification during a disruption is acceptable.

**Approach D — Formulation-Qualified Backup:** Backup is a different chemistry, different process route, or different impurity profile that meets the same functional requirement but with a distinct supply chain. This is the highest-cost, lowest-utilization backup but the most resilient to geopolitical shocks because it does not share any input supply chain with the primary. Appropriate for Tier 0 materials where the risk is correlated across the primary supply base.

**Approach E — Capacity Reservation without Active Qualification:** Buyer pays a reservation fee to a potential supplier for guaranteed capacity access in a disruption, without going through full qualification. Activation requires emergency qualification. Used as a third tier of insurance below Approaches B/C/D.

### 3.2 The Selection Matrix

| Material Tier | Recommended Approach | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Tier 0 (Existential) | A + D (Active dual-source + formulation backup) | Maximum resilience; formulation backup hedges correlated supply risk |
| Tier 1 (Critical) | B or C (Primary/backup split or capacity-qualified backup) | Cost-efficient for high-concentration materials where full dual-sourcing is uneconomic |
| Tier 2 (Important) | C (Capacity-qualified backup) | Single fully qualified primary plus a qualified backup at lower fidelity |
| Tier 3 (Manageable) | Single-source with relationship continuity | Standard procurement discipline |

The decision must also factor supplier-specific dynamics: a supplier who is itself capacity-constrained will resist Approach A; a supplier with idle capacity may welcome it; a supplier in a high-geopolitical-risk jurisdiction may prefer Approach C over A because they understand the buyer's risk. The right configuration is bilateral.

---

## 4. Qualification Acceleration Strategies

The 12-24 month qualification timeline is the binding constraint on responsiveness. Three structural levers can compress it materially.

### 4.1 Parallel Qualification with Stage-Gate Investment

The traditional model is sequential: qualify Supplier A first, then start qualifying Supplier B only after A is fully integrated. This guarantees that any disruption during A's qualification delays B's start by the full timeline. The alternative is parallel qualification of two suppliers from the outset, with a stage gate at month 6-9 that decides which to continue investing in and which to demote to a lower-tier backup.

This requires up-front qualification capex on two suppliers before either is needed for production. The cost is real but bounded — qualification costs are dominated by engineering time, not materials, and the marginal cost of qualifying a second supplier in parallel is significantly less than 2× the cost of qualifying one sequentially. The benefit is that, at any point in the program, two suppliers are partially qualified, and the time to full qualification of the backup is compressed from 18 months to perhaps 4-6 months.

### 4.2 Tiered Qualification Fidelity

Full process-of-record qualification at an advanced node is rigorous precisely because the cost of failure is high. But there are several intermediate qualification states that provide meaningful insurance at much lower cost:

- **Material-specification qualified:** Supplier can produce material meeting the published specification, but has not been integrated into the production process control system. Useful as a Tier C backup.
- **Wafer-level qualified:** Material has been tested at wafer scale with positive results, but not in volume production. Faster to ramp.
- **Reference-customer qualified:** Supplier has been qualified by a peer fab at the same node. Qualification data can sometimes be shared under NDA, compressing the buyer's qualification by 6-12 months.

For Tier 0 and Tier 1 materials, building a portfolio of suppliers at different qualification fidelities is a higher-leverage investment than over-investing in one supplier's full qualification.

### 4.3 Industry-Consortium Qualification Data

Several industry consortia — including SEMI's supplier-evaluation programs, various national materials initiatives, and customer-led consortia — share pre-qualification data among members. The economics work because every fab faces the same qualification cost, and the marginal value of any one fab's qualification data to the others is high.

Where such consortia do not exist for a given material, the buyer should consider founding one — even a small consortium of 3-5 peer fabs can dramatically reduce the qualification cost per member, and it creates a forum for sharing capacity intelligence, demand forecasts, and supplier risk assessments. CHIPS Act and EU Chips Act funding has been allocated to some of these consortia; the buyer should explore them actively.

### 4.4 Pre-Qualification of Strategic Materials

The cleanest answer to the qualification timeline is to start qualifying backup suppliers *before* they are needed for production, on a continuous rolling basis. The platform should fund a standing qualification program — perhaps 5-10% of the materials-procurement budget — that continuously moves potential backup suppliers through partial qualification, even when there is no immediate production need.

This converts the 18-month timeline from a response into a continuous operational capability. When geopolitical conditions change, the buyer has a bench of partially qualified backup suppliers ready to be promoted to full qualification in months rather than a year-plus.

The cost is recurring opex rather than crisis-driven capex. Finance is more comfortable with this because the spending is predictable and the value (option value on supply continuity) is preserved across cycles.

---

## 5. Long-Term Commitment Economics and Contract Structures

This is the section the original prompt identifies as the central problem: alternative suppliers are reluctant to commit capacity without long-term offtake agreements, but finance resists long-term commitments because they lock in costs and reduce flexibility. The resolution is not to choose between these positions but to restructure the commitments so that they share risk appropriately.

### 5.1 The Underlying Economic Problem

Suppliers in specialty gases and photoresists face a specific cost profile: high fixed cost (specialized plant, cleanrooms, analytical equipment), moderate variable cost (raw materials, energy, labor), and steep learning-curve effects at the customer end. Capacity decisions are lumpy — a new gas plant or photoresist synthesis line is a $100M-$1B investment, with lead times of 18-36 months and utilization that depends on committed offtake.

Buyers face a different cost profile: high volume variability (driven by fab utilization, technology node transitions, end-market demand), need for cost reduction over time (the industry price-curve forces it), and limited ability to predict demand 5 years out (the fab itself may not exist 5 years out, or may be running different processes).

The standard take-or-pay contract fails both sides: the supplier gets demand certainty they cannot actually use (because if the buyer's demand drops, the supplier's plant still operates and the supplier can sell elsewhere, often at lower margins), and the buyer pays for capacity they don't need.

### 5.2 A Toolkit of Optionality-Rich Contract Structures

The following structures can be deployed selectively across the material portfolio.

**Capacity Reservation Agreement (CRA).** The buyer pays a recurring reservation fee (typically 5-15% of the committed capacity's price) in exchange for guaranteed access to capacity in a disruption. The reservation fee compensates the supplier for holding capacity idle; the buyer retains the right to purchase or not purchase at the contracted price, with a cap on the upside (often 110-130% of the contract price). This is essentially a put option on capacity access.

Best for: Tier 0 and Tier 1 materials where the supplier has idle or expandable capacity and the buyer values disruption insurance over price certainty.

**Volume Commitment with Make-up Rights.** The buyer commits to a baseline volume (say 70% of expected demand) over a multi-year period, with the right to take additional volume up to a cap at a contracted price, and the right to under-take the baseline in a given year and make up the volume in a subsequent year. The supplier gets revenue visibility on the baseline; the buyer gets demand flexibility on the upside.

Best for: Tier 1 materials where the buyer has reasonable demand visibility but capacity risk is real.

**Joint Capacity Investment.** The buyer and supplier jointly invest in new capacity, with the buyer's contribution (perhaps 30-50%) treated as a prepayment that is recovered through a discounted price schedule over the contract term. This is a true partnership structure that aligns incentives across the entire investment cycle.

Best for: Tier 0 materials where the supplier is willing to expand but cannot finance the expansion alone. Often combined with government loan guarantees or co-financing from CHIPS Act-style programs.

**Pre-Purchase Storage Contract.** The buyer pays now for material that will be delivered and stored over a 12-36 month period. The supplier uses the prepayment to finance capacity expansion; the buyer stores the material at a third-party logistics provider or in their own warehouse.

Best for: Photoresists and gases with long shelf life that are non-perishable in proper storage. Also useful where the buyer's tax/balance-sheet treatment favors prepayment.

**Government-Backed Offtake Facility.** A government or multilateral agency (US EXIM, Korean K-Sure, European Investment Bank, Japan Bank for International Cooperation) provides a partial guarantee on the buyer's offtake commitment, enabling the supplier to finance expansion at lower cost. The buyer commits to a multi-year offtake; the government covers a portion of the supplier's revenue if the buyer defaults.

Best for: Tier 0 materials where the strategic importance justifies government involvement and the supplier has expansion financing as the binding constraint. CHIPS Act and similar programs have explicit authorities for this.

**Multi-Buyer Consortium Offtake.** A group of fabs (perhaps 3-7 peer companies) jointly commits to a new supplier's expansion. The commitment is allocated among the consortium members, each of which takes a share of the output. The supplier gets the full offtake they need; each buyer takes a share they can actually use.

Best for: Materials where the alternative-supplier capacity decision is large enough that no single buyer can justify it alone. Common in emerging materials categories (e.g., new EUV resist chemistries).

**Reciprocal Supply Agreement.** Where two suppliers each depend on the other for input materials or capacity, a cross-commitment structure can be negotiated that effectively provides mutual insurance. Less common but powerful where the right supplier pairs exist.

Best for: Tier 1 materials where the supplier's supply chain has correlated risks with the buyer's other suppliers.

### 5.3 The Selection Framework

| Material Tier | Supplier Capacity Situation | Recommended Contract Structure |
|---|---|---|
| Tier 0 | Existing idle capacity | Capacity Reservation Agreement |
| Tier 0 | Expansion required, supplier willing to invest | Joint Capacity Investment + Government-Backed Offtake |
| Tier 0 | Expansion required, supplier unable to invest alone | Pre-Purchase Storage + Multi-Buyer Consortium |
| Tier 1 | Existing capacity | Volume Commitment with Make-up Rights |
| Tier 1 | Expansion required | Capacity Reservation + Volume Commitment |
| Tier 2 | Standard | Volume Commitment with extension option |

The art is matching the right structure to the bilateral situation, which requires supplier-specific negotiation. The default should be the lowest-commitment structure that the supplier will accept — because every commitment the buyer makes reduces flexibility, but every commitment the supplier accepts reduces supply risk.

### 5.4 Selling the Internal Case to Finance

The argument to the CFO and treasury should be framed in three layers:

1. **Insurance premium framing.** Strategic inventory, capacity reservation fees, and joint capacity investments are insurance premiums. The cost of a six-month production halt for an advanced-node fab is typically in the billions of dollars; even a 1% probability of such a halt justifies a substantial insurance investment.

2. **Option value framing.** The optionality embedded in capacity reservation, make-up rights, and consortium offtake is not cost; it is value. The buyer is buying an option whose strike price is the cost of disruption; the premium is the reservation fee.

3. **Strategic positioning framing.** A company that has built resilient supply chains in a moment of geopolitical volatility will, in the medium term, win share from less-resilient competitors whose supply is disrupted. The resilience investment is also a competitive moat.

These framings are not mutually exclusive. Different stakeholders will respond to different framings; treasury tends to respond best to the option-value framing, while the CEO and board respond to the strategic positioning framing.

## 6. Inventory, Storage, and Demand Flexibility Buffers

### 6.1 Strategic Inventory Posture

The semiconductor industry's just-in-time inventory discipline has produced enormous working-capital efficiency and is correctly the default. For Tier 3 materials, just-in-time is the right model. For Tier 0 and Tier 1 materials, the model needs adjustment.

| Material Tier | Target Inventory | Storage Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Tier 0 (Existential) | 6-12 months consumption | Dedicated on-site or partner warehouse; for gases, supplier-owned on-site storage with consignment |
| Tier 1 (Critical) | 3-6 months consumption | Mixed on-site, regional warehouse, and consignment at supplier |
| Tier 2 (Important) | 1-3 months consumption | Pipeline + buffer |
| Tier 3 (Manageable) | Just-in-time | Standard |

The cost of strategic inventory is real but bounded. Photoresists are expensive but stable; noble gases are inexpensive but require specialized storage; most specialty gases have well-developed supplier-owned consignment models. For many Tier 0 and Tier 1 materials, supplier-owned consignment inventory can provide the resilience benefit without the balance-sheet impact of buyer-owned inventory — the buyer pays only when material is consumed, but the supplier holds the inventory for guaranteed access.
